design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (reported to the MOOSE and PRISMA guidelines; no protocol or registration mentioned) of within-participant, placebo-controlled crossover studies in which healthy adults received one acute subanesthetic intravenous dose of racemic ketamine or S-ketamine and were rated on the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) or the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Outcomes: total, positive and negative symptom scores under ketamine versus saline, pooled as standardized mean change scores (ketamine mean minus placebo mean, divided by the SD of the within-person difference computed with an assumed ketamine–placebo correlation of 0.5). 36 studies (22 BPRS, 14 PANSS) with 725 participants; 3 studies in people with schizophrenia were summarized without pooling. Subgroup analyses by blinding, preparation, infusion method and same-day versus different-day conditions; meta-regression on study mean age and sex.
can_establish: The average size, across published laboratory challenge studies, of the within-person increase in clinician-rated psychotic-like symptoms (BPRS or PANSS total, positive and negative scores) during or shortly after one intravenous subanesthetic dose of racemic ketamine or S-ketamine compared with saline in healthy adults, taken at each study’s highest dose and peak rating, and how consistently such increases appear across studies.
cannot_establish: Effects at a typical rather than peak time and dose, a dose–response or concentration–effect relation, how long symptoms last after the session, effects by other routes (no non-intravenous study had usable data) or in people given ketamine for depression or pain, a pooled estimate for people with schizophrenia (3 studies, not pooled), whether a bolus causes larger positive-symptom effects than an infusion alone (a between-study comparison resting on 2 infusion-only studies), or anything about lasting symptoms or the risk of a psychotic disorder.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Three authors independently searched MEDLINE (1946 to 3 February 2020), Embase (1974 to 3 February 2020) and PsycINFO (1806 to 27 January 2020), hand-searched meta-analyses and reviews, and contacted study authors for missing full texts, subscale scores or item lists (Methods › Selection Procedures). Participants in the pooled studies were healthy adults in laboratory challenge studies; how the primary studies recruited them is not described in the main text.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies of healthy participants (for the schizophrenia synthesis, people with a DSM or ICD-10 diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder) given acute subanesthetic intravenous racemic, S- or R-ketamine, with a within-participant placebo crossover and BPRS or PANSS total, positive or negative scores from which a mean difference and its deviation could be estimated. Excluded: no placebo condition; no total, positive or negative scores; missing measures in either condition; no original data; no SD or standard error; no more than 2 participants per group; another drug given together with ketamine (Methods › Selection Criteria for the Meta-analysis of Ketamine’s Effects in Healthy Volunteers). A negative BPRS score had to contain blunted affect, emotional withdrawal and motor retardation; for the positive score the criterion names conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour, unusual thought content and suspiciousness (Methods › Additional Symptom Subdomain Inclusion Criteria for Both Meta-analyses; see reporting issues).
sample.demographics: 725 healthy volunteers; mean (SD) age 28.3 (3.6) years (study mean ages 21.7 to 39.6 in the Table); reported as 533 men (73.6%) and 192 women (26.5%) (Results › Retrieved Studies for the Meta-analysis of Healthy Volunteers). Study sizes 8 to 93 (median 16; 7 studies with 10 or fewer participants); 11 of the 32 studies that reported sex enrolled men only, and 4 studies with 107 participants did not report sex (Table; editors’ tally). People with schizophrenia: 48 in 3 studies (13, 17 and 18 participants; mean ages 31.3 to 34.7 years).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; dropouts within the primary studies are not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Only within-person placebo crossover studies were pooled (at full text, 9 independent-group studies and 22 studies without placebo were excluded), and 25 studies were excluded because raw data could not be provided (Figure 1), which could bias the pooled estimates if those studies differed. For each study the review took the highest dose tested and the rating time with the largest ketamine score, so the pooled values describe peak effects (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 4th paragraph). Several pooled studies were designed to test ketamine together with another drug (lorazepam, haloperidol, lamotrigine, naltrexone, nicotine, amphetamine, a glycine transporter inhibitor; thiopental as a comparison), and some titles name patient groups (recovering ethanol-dependent patients, schizophrenia, depression) although these studies are listed among healthy volunteers; the main text does not say which conditions or subgroups were extracted. Only 5 studies excluded people with prior ketamine exposure, and most did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph). At least 8 of the 36 pooled studies list a review author (Krystal, D’Souza or Driesen) as first or named author in the reference list.

exposure.measurement: Ketamine given in the laboratory under each primary study’s protocol; intravenous in every pooled study (two intranasal esketamine studies were found but had no usable data). Racemic ketamine or S-ketamine; no R-ketamine study appears among the pooled studies. Doses per study are given only in Supplement eTables 5 and 6, which were not read; the highest dose was taken from multi-dose studies (Methods › Recorded Variables, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them: one intravenous administration per session, either a bolus followed by a continuous infusion (19 of the 21 positive-symptom studies) or a continuous infusion alone (2 of the 21). The authors put the human doses in these studies at approximately 0.65 mg/kg (Discussion › Association of Age and Sex With Ketamine-Induced Psychopathology) and compare them with the approximately 0.5 mg/kg intravenous dose used in depression trials (Discussion › Implications for Therapeutic Use of Ketamine). Where reported (17 of 36 studies), symptoms were rated 1 to 120 minutes after the start of the infusion (Table, last column).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level. Co-administration of another drug was an exclusion criterion, but several pooled studies were drug-interaction designs and the main text does not say which arms were used; most primary studies did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use, and participants’ other drug use is not reported in the main text.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported in the main text (each study’s exclusion criteria are listed in Supplement eTables 5 and 6, not read).

comparison.controls: Each participant’s own saline condition (35 studies; placebo not reported for 1), in a crossover; in 2 studies the ketamine and placebo conditions were on the same day.
comparison.matching: Within-person. Per the Table, condition order was randomized in 30 of 36 studies and not in 6; 27 studies were double-blind, 5 single-blind, 3 unblinded and 1 did not report blinding.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant to the within-person contrast itself, but differences between study samples (prior ketamine or other drug experience, psychosis proneness, family history of psychosis, personality) were not analysed; only study mean age and percentage of men were examined as moderators.

outcomes.instruments: BPRS (any version: 16-, 18-, 20- and 24-item versions were mixed and the version was often not stated) and PANSS, clinician or researcher ratings of psychotic-like symptoms during or shortly after the infusion: total score; positive score (BPRS conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour and unusual thought content, with or without suspiciousness; PANSS positive scale); negative score (BPRS blunted affect, emotional withdrawal and motor retardation; PANSS negative scale). Where a study rated several time points, the point with the largest ketamine score was used, with the placebo score at the matching time.
outcomes.validity_norms: BPRS and PANSS are validated measures of symptom severity in schizophrenia; in healthy volunteers during a drug challenge they have no norms. For clinical context the authors relate the average total PANSS difference (18.40 points) to Clinical Global Impression severity categories in schizophrenia, citing Leucht et al. (2005), an extrapolation from patients to volunteers who start near the bottom of the scale.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychotomimetic or schizophrenia-like symptoms are operationalized as higher BPRS or PANSS scores under ketamine than under saline in the same person, expressed as a standardized mean change. No outcome after the session was analysed, so nothing is measured as a lasting effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three primary pooled outcomes (total, positive, negative), plus 12 subgroup comparisons (blinding, preparation, infusion method and same-day versus different-day, each for three outcomes), 6 meta-regressions (age and sex for three outcomes), 3 BPRS-versus-PANSS comparisons and one positive-versus-negative comparison, all at P < .05 two-tailed; 2 of the 12 subgroup comparisons were significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Review level: two independent investigators extracted the data and two scored risk of bias. Study level: 27 of 36 studies were double-blind per the Table; the authors note that ketamine’s obvious dissociative effects make blinding of participants and staff very difficult, and no data on blinding integrity are reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects models (REML, metafor 1.9-9 in R 3.3.1); standardized mean change with r = 0.5 (sensitivity analyses with r = 0.1 and 0.7 in the supplement, not read); no small-sample correction is mentioned; tau-squared and prediction intervals not reported. Healthy volunteers, ketamine versus placebo: total SMD 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.77), 25 studies, 491 participants, I2 75.7%, Q 96.57 (df 24); positive 1.55 (1.29 to 1.81), 21 studies, 513 participants, I2 74.9%, Q 81.40 (df 20); negative 1.16 (0.96 to 1.35), 22 studies, 527 participants, I2 64.6%, Q 66.55 (df 21); all P < .001. Leave-one-out ranges 1.44 to 1.55, 1.47 to 1.60 and 1.11 to 1.19. Egger tests z = 4.27, 5.06 and 5.12 (all P < .001); trim-and-fill added 3, 1 and 2 studies, giving 1.37 (1.07 to 1.67), 1.49 (1.18 to 1.80) and 1.09 (0.89 to 1.30). Positive minus negative: 0.36 (0.12 to 0.61), z = 2.90, P = .004. Infusion method, positive symptoms: bolus plus infusion 1.63 (1.36 to 1.90), 19 studies, versus infusion alone 0.84 (0.35 to 1.33), 2 studies, P = .006; not significant for total or negative symptoms. Same-day versus different-day, total symptoms: 2.29 (1.69 to 2.89), 2 studies, versus 1.39 (1.12 to 1.66), 17 studies, P = .007; not significant for positive or negative. Blinding and preparation: no significant subgroup differences. Editors’ calculation (REML tau-squared from the study-level SMDs and 95% CIs printed in Figures 2 to 4, SE = CI width / 3.92, 95% prediction interval with t on k − 2 df; this reconstruction reproduces the published pooled estimates and CIs to two decimals): tau about 0.57, 0.51 and 0.36; prediction intervals about 0.28 to 2.72 (total), 0.44 to 2.65 (positive) and 0.39 to 1.93 (negative).
analysis.covariates: None in the main models. Random-effects meta-regressions on study mean age (24 total, 20 positive, 20 negative studies) and percentage of men (22, 19 and 19 studies) found no significant moderation; these are study-level (ecological) analyses over study mean ages of 22 to 40 years.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states that it followed the MOOSE and PRISMA reporting guidelines.
analysis.selective_reporting: The peak rating time and highest dose were chosen per study by design, which the authors say makes the pooled values likely the largest effects seen. Significant Egger tests for all three outcomes are reported in Results but not in the abstract or Key Points. Sensitivity analyses for the assumed correlation, subgroup heterogeneity statistics, funnel plots and per-study risk-of-bias judgments are only in the supplement, which was not read.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Subgroup contrasts rest on as few as 2 studies (infusion alone, positive symptoms; same-day conditions, total symptoms), so they are imprecise and confounded with everything else that differed between those studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy volunteers, one intravenous subanesthetic dose of ketamine raised BPRS or PANSS scores relative to saline in every pooled study, with large average standardized mean changes at each study’s peak rating and highest dose (total 1.50, positive 1.55, negative 1.16), larger for positive than for negative symptoms (difference 0.36), with high heterogeneity (I2 65% to 76%; editors’ prediction intervals from about 0.3 to 2.7), significant small-study asymmetry in all three analyses, and trim-and-fill estimates slightly lower but still large. Positive-symptom effects were larger in 19 bolus-plus-infusion studies than in 2 infusion-only studies, and total-symptom effects larger in 2 same-day studies than in 17 different-day studies; neither contrast held for the other outcomes. Three small studies in schizophrenia were not pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say that bolus doses should be avoided in therapeutic use to minimize transient positive symptoms, and the conclusions call a slow infusion without a bolus preferable (Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Conclusions). This rests on a between-study comparison of 19 with 2 studies in healthy volunteers (SMDs 1.02 and 0.50 for the two infusion-only studies, Figure 3), confounded by dose, rate, timing of ratings and laboratory, with no difference for total or negative symptoms and no data from patients. The abstract states the subgroup results causally (a bolus and a same-day design increased the effects). The Key Points describe a meaningful increase in symptoms in patients with schizophrenia, although no meta-analysis was possible in schizophrenia and one of the two studies that rated negative symptoms found no increase. The abstract says age and sex did not moderate outcomes, from ecological meta-regressions over study mean ages of 22 to 40 years. The abstract and Key Points omit the significant Egger tests. The abstract's heterogeneity figure (an I2 range of 77% to 83%) matches none of the three values in the Results and overstates the inconsistency the review measured. The text calls the symptoms transient throughout, but the review analysed no rating after the session. The authors’ statement that the findings support ketamine as a pharmacological model of schizophrenia is their interpretation of symptom-scale changes. Against this, the discussion states plainly that blinding is difficult and that selecting peak values inflates the estimates.

timeline.event: Krystal et al.: placebo-controlled ketamine challenge in healthy volunteers with BPRS ratings; cited in this review’s introduction but not among the pooled studies (no reason given in the main text).
Lahti et al.: ketamine challenge in people with schizophrenia; excluded from this review’s schizophrenia synthesis as one of 7 studies with overlapping data sets.
Malhotra et al. (Neuropsychopharmacology): healthy (16) and schizophrenia (13) samples, both used by this review.
Newcomer et al.: pooled in this review’s total- and positive-symptom analyses (15 participants).
Lahti et al. (normal and schizophrenic volunteers): its schizophrenia sample (17) is in this review’s narrative synthesis.
Dickerson et al.: the largest pooled study (93 participants, single-blind), with among the smallest effects (total 0.87, positive 0.79, negative 0.51; Figures 2 to 4).
This review: 36 studies, 725 healthy volunteers; 3 studies in schizophrenia summarized.
Ait Bentaleb et al.: meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies of ketamine in healthy volunteers (a different outcome; appraised in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: The review cites no earlier meta-analysis of these outcomes. Its pooled estimates include studies the encyclopedia cites separately, so those studies are not independent replications of this review: Newcomer et al. (1999) is reference 31 and sits in both the total-symptom and the positive-symptom analyses, and Malhotra et al. (1997), reference 25, is pooled with 16 healthy participants and is a companion report from the laboratory of Malhotra et al. (1996); Krystal et al. (1994) is not among the 36 and appears only as reference 5 in a meta-regression list. At least 8 of the 36 pooled studies come from one laboratory group that includes three of the review's authors (overlapping evidence, METHODS §6.3). Effects in schizophrenia, the dose–response relation and the time course after the session remain unsynthesized.

(1998, 1999, 2003, 2005, 2006) — so the review extracted and appraised its own authors’ studies; those 8 carry a large share of the pooled samples, and no procedure for handling this is described. what_would_settle_it: A randomized within-person study comparing a bolus plus infusion with an infusion alone at the same total dose, with measured plasma concentrations, an active placebo, BPRS or PANSS and dissociation ratings at fixed times during and after the session, and a check of blinding; and an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing challenge studies modelling dose, plasma concentration, rating time, prior drug experience and sex.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (healthy volunteers; schizophrenia), intervention (acute subanesthetic intravenous ketamine), comparator (within-person placebo) and outcomes (BPRS or PANSS total, positive, negative) are specified.
No protocol, registration or statement that methods were fixed in advance; MOOSE and PRISMA are reporting guidelines, not a protocol.
Only within-participant placebo crossover studies were eligible (independent-group studies were excluded at full text), but the choice of design is not explained.

Three databases with dates and keywords, independent searching by three authors, hand-searching of reviews, author contact and a search about 4 months before publication; no trial registries or grey literature, and no reference-list searching of included studies. No language or publication-type restriction is stated.
Three authors searched independently and the same three selected the final studies (Methods › Selection Procedures); how disagreements were resolved is not described.
Two independent investigators extracted study-level data (Abstract › Data Extraction and Synthesis).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the main text gives counts of full-text exclusions by reason (Figure 1) and names a few excluded studies (7 overlapping schizophrenia data sets; 2 intranasal studies without data); a list may be in Supplement eMethods 1 (Studies and Data Not Included in Meta-analysis), which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The Table gives size, age, sex, blinding, randomization, placebo, subscales and timing of ratings; doses, infusion protocols and exclusion criteria are only in eTables 5 and 6 (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle-Ottawa scale (a tool for cohort studies, applied with a summary-score cut-off of 7) and the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, scored by two investigators; the across-study summary rates performance and detection bias low although the Table lists 3 unblinded, 5 single-blind and 1 unreported study and the authors say blinding is very difficult; per-study judgments are in the supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text.

REML random-effects models for within-person standardized mean changes, a sensitivity analysis for the assumed correlation, a multivariate model for the positive-versus-negative comparison, and leave-one-out analyses; selecting each study’s peak value is a data choice the authors disclose.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Subgroup analyses by blinding status (double-blind versus single-blind or unblinded) for all three outcomes; the 8 studies rated high risk on the Newcastle-Ottawa scale were not analysed separately.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion considers the difficulty of blinding, expectancy and possible unblinding (including as an explanation of the same-day result) and the inflation from selecting peak values; these points are not carried into the abstract’s therapeutic recommendation.
Q and I2 for every pool, subgroup analyses and meta-regressions, and a discussion of design factors; the authors note that subgroups did not explain most of the heterogeneity.

Egger tests, funnel plots and trim-and-fill for all three outcomes, with adjusted estimates and a comment that negative studies may be missing (Results); not mentioned in the discussion, abstract or Key Points.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and extensive author disclosures are reported; the overlap between review authors and authors of included studies is not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from Supplement eMethods 1, which was not read. With item 2 a critical flaw (no protocol) and the other critical items met or partly met, AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; if eMethods 1 does not list the excluded studies with reasons, the rating becomes critically low. The primary studies are within-person, mostly randomized and double-blind laboratory experiments, so the direction of the acute effect is well supported; what limits the review is the selection of peak values, the reliance on standardized mean changes with an assumed correlation, high heterogeneity, small-study asymmetry and subgroup contrasts resting on 2 studies. The review may be cited for the presence and approximate size of acute BPRS and PANSS increases during intravenous challenge in healthy adults (with the peak-value caveat and the prediction interval); it should not be cited for a dose or infusion-method effect, for effects in schizophrenia, for therapeutic practice, or for the duration of symptoms.

key_findings.finding: 36 within-person placebo-controlled studies with 725 healthy volunteers were pooled (22 using the BPRS and 14 the PANSS), from 8464 records screened and 126 full texts assessed; 90 full texts were excluded (28 duplicate data, 25 raw data not available, 22 no placebo condition, 9 independent-group design, 3 no intravenous administration or fewer than 2 participants, 2 incorrect BPRS items, 1 additional compound given). Ketamine was given intravenously in all pooled studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Retrieved Studies for the Meta-analysis of Healthy Volunteers, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (flowchart, read from the image); Table

key_findings.finding: Total symptoms (25 studies, 491 healthy volunteers): SMD 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.77), P < .001, ketamine versus placebo; leave-one-out range 1.44 to 1.55; I2 75.7% (Q 96.57, df 24); Egger z = 4.27, P < .001; trim-and-fill added 3 studies, adjusted SMD 1.37 (1.07 to 1.67). Study-level SMDs ranged from 0.49 (−0.17 to 1.15) to 3.51 (2.15 to 4.86).
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 (values printed in the forest plot)

key_findings.finding: Positive symptoms (21 studies, 513 healthy volunteers): SMD 1.55 (1.29 to 1.81), P < .001; leave-one-out 1.47 to 1.60; I2 74.9% (Q 81.40, df 20); Egger z = 5.06, P < .001; trim-and-fill added 1 study, adjusted 1.49 (1.18 to 1.80). Study-level SMDs ranged from 0.50 (−0.24 to 1.23) to 4.66 (3.15 to 6.17).
key_findings.locator: Results › Positive Psychotic Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms (22 studies, 527 healthy volunteers): SMD 1.16 (0.96 to 1.35), P < .001; leave-one-out 1.11 to 1.19; I2 64.6% (Q 66.55, df 21); Egger z = 5.12, P < .001; trim-and-fill added 2 studies, adjusted 1.09 (0.89 to 1.30). Study-level SMDs ranged from 0.45 (−0.10 to 1.00) to 2.30 (1.33 to 3.26).
key_findings.locator: Results › Negative Symptoms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 4

key_findings.finding: The association was larger for positive than for negative symptoms: difference 0.36 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.61), z = 2.90, P = .004, from a multivariate model assuming a within-study correlation of 0.5 between positive and negative scores (sensitivity analyses with 0.1 and 0.7 in the supplement). BPRS and PANSS gave no significantly different results for any domain.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Positive and Negative Effect Sizes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes are standardized mean change scores: the ketamine–placebo mean difference divided by the square root of SD(ketamine)² + SD(placebo)² − 2r·SD(ketamine)·SD(placebo), with r set to 0.5 for every study (sensitivity analyses with r = 0.1 and 0.7 in the supplement). For each study the highest dose and the rating time with the largest ketamine score were used, so the authors describe the pooled values as likely the largest effects seen.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (equation read from the image); Methods › Recorded Variables, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: A within-person standardized change is not directly comparable with a between-group SMD (for example from a parallel-group trial), and its size depends on the assumed correlation.

key_findings.finding: Infusion method: for positive symptoms, studies giving a bolus followed by a continuous infusion (19 studies) showed a larger effect than those giving a continuous infusion alone (2 studies): SMD 1.63 (1.36 to 1.90) versus 0.84 (0.35 to 1.33), P = .006. For total symptoms, 1.55 (1.23 to 1.88) versus 1.27 (0.73 to 1.81), and for negative symptoms 1.19 (0.96 to 1.41) versus 1.06 (0.71 to 1.40), the differences were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Positive Psychotic Symptoms › Infusion Method; Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms › Infusion Method; Results › Negative Symptoms › Infusion Method
key_findings.note: The two infusion-only positive-symptom studies are Krystal et al. (2003), SMD 1.02 (0.55 to 1.50), and Micallef et al. (2002), 0.50 (−0.24 to 1.23), from Figure 3; this is a between-study comparison confounded by dose, rate, timing and laboratory.

key_findings.finding: Same-day versus different-day conditions: for total symptoms, 2 single-day studies (Thiebes et al., 2017; Kraguljac et al., 2017) gave a larger effect than 17 multiple-day studies, SMD 2.29 (1.69 to 2.89) versus 1.39 (1.12 to 1.66), P = .007; for positive symptoms 1.54 (1.19 to 1.89) versus 1.53 (1.15 to 1.90) and for negative symptoms 1.01 (0.56 to 1.47) versus 1.16 (0.94 to 1.39), no significant difference. The authors suggest unblinding or better control of day-to-day variation as explanations.
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms › Single-Day vs Multiple-Day Studies; Positive Psychotic Symptoms › Single-Day vs Multiple-Day Studies; Negative Symptoms › Single-Day vs Multiple-Day Studies; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding and preparation did not change the pooled effects significantly. Total symptoms: unblinded or single-blind 1.71 (1.02 to 2.39) versus double-blind 1.45 (1.15 to 1.75); racemic ketamine 1.40 (1.12 to 1.68) versus S-ketamine 2.03 (1.15 to 2.92). Positive: 1.32 (0.96 to 1.67) versus 1.68 (1.30 to 2.07); racemic 1.50 (1.17 to 1.82) versus S-ketamine 1.70 (1.23 to 2.18). Negative: 0.98 (0.63 to 1.34) versus 1.29 (1.09 to 1.50); racemic 1.13 (0.90 to 1.36) versus S-ketamine 1.25 (0.86 to 1.64).
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms, Positive Psychotic Symptoms and Negative Symptoms › Ketamine Preparation and Blinding Method subsections

key_findings.finding: Meta-regressions on study mean age and percentage of men showed no significant moderation of total, positive or negative effects; the included studies were of adults only, with study mean ages of 22 to 40 years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Positive Psychotic Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Negative Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Association of Age and Sex With Ketamine-Induced Psychopathology

key_findings.finding: People with schizophrenia: after 7 studies with overlapping data sets were excluded, 3 studies remained (Malhotra et al., 1997, 13 participants; Lahti et al., 2001, 17; Malhotra et al., 1998, 18), too few to pool; change scores were accepted here. Both studies reporting total BPRS found a significant increase with ketamine; both reporting positive symptoms found a significant transient increase; of the two reporting negative symptoms, one (Malhotra et al., 1998) found an increase and one (Lahti et al., 2001) did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of Ketamine in Patients With Schizophrenia, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table (Schizophrenia rows)

key_findings.finding: For clinical context the authors report an average mean difference of 18.40 points in total PANSS between the placebo and ketamine conditions, which they equate, were it to occur in a patient with schizophrenia, to a change from mild illness to markedly ill on the Clinical Global Impression scale (citing Leucht et al., 2005).
key_findings.note: The number of studies behind the 18.40 average and whether it is weighted are not stated; the equivalence is an extrapolation from patients to healthy volunteers.

key_findings.finding: Study characteristics (Table): 27 of 36 studies double-blind, 5 single-blind, 3 unblinded and 1 not reported; order randomized in 30 and not in 6; saline placebo in 35. Time from the start of the infusion to the symptom rating was reported for 17 studies (1 to 120 minutes) and not for 19. Only 5 studies excluded people with prior ketamine exposure, and most did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use.
key_findings.locator: Table (Blinded, Randomized, Placebo condition and Length of ketamine infusion before symptom assessment columns; editors’ tally); Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Read with the peak-value rule (key finding 5), this timing column fixes what the pooled figures describe: symptoms at their height during the session or at the end of the infusion, with nothing measured after it. For 19 of the 36 studies the timing is not reported at all.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias of the included studies: on the Newcastle-Ottawa scale (score of at least 7 taken as low risk), 8 studies were at high risk, mainly for not documenting aspects of the design; the Cochrane tool across studies gave unclear risk for selection bias and low risk for performance, detection, attrition and reporting bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of Bias Across Studies, 1st paragraph; Methods › Risk of Bias

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity and its limits: the authors attribute part of the inconsistency to design factors (bolus plus infusion roughly doubling positive-symptom effects; same-day designs), but heterogeneity stayed moderate to high within most subgroups; dose and fasting status could not be examined because few studies reported them, and BPRS versions with 16, 18, 20 and 24 items were mixed. Editors’ calculation from Figures 2 to 4 (method under analysis): 95% prediction intervals about 0.28 to 2.72 (total), 0.44 to 2.65 (positive) and 0.39 to 1.93 (negative).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st paragraph; Figures 2 to 4 (editors’ calculation)

key_findings.finding: Relevance to therapeutic use, as the authors put it: the approximately 0.5 mg/kg intravenous dose used to treat depression is similar to the doses in the pooled studies; they cite psychotic symptoms in depressed patients (mean BPRS score 12.6) slightly above the average mean score across the pooled BPRS studies (7.5), and recommend avoiding a bolus. The review contains no pooled data from patients treated for depression or pain.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Implications for Therapeutic Use of Ketamine; Conclusions
key_findings.note: Which BPRS score (total or positive) and which study the 12.6 comes from are not stated (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: In the Table, the sex split does not add up to the sample size in three rows: Krystal et al. (1998), 23 participants but 19 men and 11 women; Morgan et al. (2011), 16 but 10 and 8; Powers et al. (2015), 19 but 10 and 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: The per-study sex data used in the sex meta-regressions cannot be checked from the Table.

reporting_issues.issue: The reported 533 men (73.6%) equals 725 minus the 192 women in the Table; the men listed in the Table sum to 436, and 4 studies with 107 participants report sex as not reported, so the figure counts all of them as men or uses data not shown (editors’ arithmetic). 533 of 725 is 73.5%, not 73.6%, and the reported mean age (28.3) is not reproduced by the Table’s study means (unweighted 28.1, weighted 27.6).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Retrieved Studies for the Meta-analysis of Healthy Volunteers; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion of men in the pooled evidence is at most about 74% and may be lower; claims about who was studied should give the Table-based figures or say the sex of 107 participants is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says that of the two same-day studies one was unblinded (reference 29, Thiebes) and the other single-blind with randomized order (reference 30, Kraguljac); the Table gives the reverse: Thiebes single-blind and randomized, Kraguljac unblinded and not randomized.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels are swapped; the explanation by unblinding still applies to both studies, which were not double-blind.

reporting_issues.issue: The across-study Cochrane assessment rates performance and detection bias low, while the Table lists 3 unblinded, 5 single-blind and 1 study without blinding information, and the authors state that ketamine’s effects make blinding very difficult.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Risk of Bias Across Studies; Table; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The review’s risk-of-bias summary understates the threat from functional unblinding; it should not be cited as showing low risk of bias.

reporting_issues.issue: The positive-symptom criterion says studies were included if they had more than 3 positive items, listing 4 items, but studies using the 3-item positive score (positive (2) in the Table footnote), such as Kraguljac et al. (2017), are in the positive-symptom analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Additional Symptom Subdomain Inclusion Criteria for Both Meta-analyses; Table footnote; Results › Positive Psychotic Symptoms, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The criterion was probably at least 3 items; positive scores pooled across studies did not all use the same items.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation errors in study lists: the list of 19 bolus-plus-infusion positive-symptom studies includes reference 64 (Lahti et al., 1995, a schizophrenia study excluded for overlapping data) and omits reference 3 (Krystal et al., 2005); the age meta-regression list for total symptoms starts with reference 5 (Krystal et al., 1994, not an included study), apparently for reference 25; Figure 2 labels D’Souza et al. (2012) with reference number 32 (Krystal et al., 2006) instead of 51; the list of studies that did not exclude concurrent psychotropic drug use includes references 80 and 81, which are not included studies.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Positive Psychotic Symptoms › Infusion Method; Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2; Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the pooled counts are consistent with the Table and the forest plots, but the printed reference lists cannot be used as they stand to audit the subgroups.

reporting_issues.issue: The two non-intravenous studies found by the search are described as using inhaled administration, but both cited studies (references 62 and 63) gave intranasal esketamine.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Retrieved Studies for the Meta-analysis of Healthy Volunteers, 1st paragraph; references 62 and 63
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no non-intravenous study contributed data.

reporting_issues.issue: The same-day versus different-day comparison for total symptoms covers 2 + 17 = 19 of the 25 total-symptom studies; 6 studies (Krystal et al., 2006; Grent-’t-Jong et al., 2018; Höflich et al., 2015; Abdallah et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2011; Nagels et al., 2011) are not assigned, without explanation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Total Psychopathological Symptoms › Single-Day vs Multiple-Day Studies
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup result (P = .007) rests on 19 studies, and the reason for leaving 6 out is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The flowchart leaves 36 studies after full-text review (126 − 90), but the review uses 38 reports: the 36 healthy-volunteer studies plus Lahti et al. (2001) and Malhotra et al. (1998) for schizophrenia (Malhotra et al., 1997, contributes to both).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the flow of studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of psychotic symptoms in depressed patients (mean BPRS score 12.6) with the average mean score across the pooled BPRS studies (7.5) does not say which BPRS score (total or positive) is meant or which study gives 12.6; the sentence cites references 78 and 79 nearby.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Implications for Therapeutic Use of Ketamine
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot be checked and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: For positive symptoms with infusion alone the P value is printed as P < .008, an unusual threshold, beside the subgroup comparison P = .006.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Positive Psychotic Symptoms › Infusion Method
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the subgroup estimate (0.84, 0.35 to 1.33) is reproduced by pooling the two studies in Figure 3 (editors’ check).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports significant inconsistency between studies with an I2 range of 77% to 83%; the Results give I2 of 75.7% (total), 74.9% (positive) and 64.6% (negative), and no value of 77% or 83% appears anywhere in the main text or in any subgroup figure printed there.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract > Results; Results > Total Psychopathological Symptoms, Positive Psychotic Symptoms and Negative Symptoms, 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure a reader of the abstract alone carries away overstates the review's own measured inconsistency, and two of the three Results values sit in the review's own medium band (25% to 75%) rather than the high band the abstract's range implies. Heterogeneity should be cited from the Results.
